subtype: Approach: uses one method for every problem out of habit [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Sangeeta has to make a poster for the arts fest. She opens the colour-coded timetable app she uses for exams: sketch 9 to 10, colours 10 to 12, lettering 2 to 3. She sits down at nine with a pencil, and nothing comes.
Wednesday. The same block has moved forward twice. "Idea generation, ten minutes," the app says. She stares at a blank page. Nandini asks, "Want to just doodle for a bit?" "It's not in the schedule."
Friday. The sheet is still empty and every block on the timetable is red. Sangeeta rubs her eyes and opens the app again to move the blocks once more.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta have to make for the arts fest?
qa.a: Sangeeta has to make a poster.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta feel when saying that doodling is not in the schedule?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels tense and stuck, holding tightly to the timetable even though it has not helped.

qa.q: What different approach might suit the poster better?
qa.a: Sangeeta could start with loose doodles for a short time, since creative work often starts better without fixed blocks.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel watching the timetable move again?
qa.a: Nandini offered to doodle, so may feel concerned and a bit helpless watching Sangeeta turn down a loose start.

grounding: A student who likes detailed timetables uses one for creative work, where a loose start would suit better, and feels blocked.

subtype: Approach: uses one method for every problem out of habit [Pitfall]
passage: Abhinav, you're stuck on your short film script? Let me tell your Thomas Uncle's story. In college, I was the timetable king. Every exam, every assignment, planned to the half hour, and it worked beautifully for engineering. Then I joined the drama club and had to write a one-act play. What did I do? A timetable. "Monday 6 to 7: Scene 1. Tuesday 6 to 7: Scene 2." Monday at six I sat down, and nothing came. At seven I had two lines and felt like a failure. Tuesday, the same. For two weeks I kept the timetable and wrote almost nothing. Creative work doesn't come on schedule. My friend finally said, "Just scribble anything, anywhere." I'd never tried that. I'd used one method for everything.

qa.q: What did young Thomas write in his timetable for Monday?
How did young Thomas feel at seven on Monday?
qa.a: Young Thomas felt blocked, frustrated and like a failure, with only two lines written.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Thomas have changed course?
qa.a: After the first blocked evening; trying a loose start, like scribbling ideas anywhere, would have suited the play better.

qa.q: How might Thomas's friend have felt watching him struggle?
qa.a: The friend probably felt concerned and a little impatient, which is why they suggested scribbling anything.

grounding: An elder recalls using detailed timetables even for creative writing, where a loose start would have suited better, and feeling blocked.

subtype: Approach: uses one method for every problem out of habit [Pitfall]
passage: The poster design competition closed on Friday, and Suraj had only three evenings, between his internship and the metro ride home. He did what always worked for him: a timetable. "Tuesday 8 to 9: concept. Wednesday 8 to 9: layout. Thursday 8 to 9: colours." On Tuesday at eight he sat at his desk, timer running, and stared at a blank screen. No concept came. At nine he had nothing. On Wednesday he forced a layout for an idea he didn't like. His friend Bidisha, an art student, saw it on Thursday. "You look miserable. What if you just doodled on the metro tomorrow?" Suraj frowned. Timetables had never failed him before. But the screen was still empty, and the deadline was one day away.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel staring at the blank screen?
qa.a: He felt blocked and frustrated, since the timetable that always worked wasn't producing ideas.

qa.q: Which approach would suit a creative task like this better?
qa.a: A loose start, like doodling on the metro as Bidisha suggests, to let ideas come before planning the layout.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see Suraj's approach?
qa.a: Bidisha sees that he looks miserable and suggests a looser way, probably from knowing how creative work goes.

grounding: A student who loves detailed timetables uses one even for creative design, where a loose start would suit better, and feels blocked.
